{"body":"Part of #35 (section 3, enhancement 6). Prerequisite for the tile-grid runtime sub-issue.

## The gap

The mesh path draws COLOURED geometry only (`VertexPositionColor`) — right for panels and bars, useless for anything wearing art. So a terrain of 4,000 visible tiles must be 4,000 **sprite entities**: 4,000 culled, prepped, sorted, batched quads, every frame. The cost is not the drawing; it is the bookkeeping per thing.

## The capability (proven in the game, ready to port)

`DrawComponent.TexturedVertices` (`VertexPositionColorTexture[]` — each corner knows where on the tileset it samples) + a `BasicEffect.TextureEnabled`/PointClamp branch in `MasterRenderSystem`. A whole 16x16 chunk of terrain becomes ONE draw: one thing culled, one thing sorted. This is the enabling half of the game's measured 5.0 → 1.5 ms frame (the tile system that exploits it is a separate sub-issue; the capability is pure rendering and stands alone). It is also where per-vertex distortions live — including the skew/shear effects #39 documents as impossible-as-a-sprite-flag.

## The cliff this PR also writes down (it fails SILENTLY on web)

Index buffers come in 16-bit and 32-bit. Past **65,536 vertices** the index helper quietly falls back to 32-bit — which the **Reach profile the web build runs on rejects**. Failure mode: desktop renders fine, the browser renders NOTHING — no exception, no log line, a blank canvas. *Witch v Necromancer* hit this designing its map page: 113k world cells had to be run-length merged into 13.4k vertices precisely to stay under the cliff, and only a code comment knew why.

The vendored `DrawComponent` extends the existing ceiling check to the textured buffer; the premise makes the cliff documented knowledge so the next person designs under it instead of discovering it from a blank canvas in Chrome.

## Delivery

- [ ] Port `TexturedVertices` / `IsTexturedMesh` / `MeshVertexCount` and the extended 16-bit-index ceiling check into `Component/Draw/DrawComponent.cs`
- [ ] Port the textured branch into `System/Draw/MasterRenderSystem.cs` (`BasicEffect.TextureEnabled`, PointClamp — pixel art must not bilinear-smear)
- [ ] Premises entry: "a mesh may be textured" + the 16-bit / Reach ceiling, with the web failure mode spelled out
- [ ] Test: a textured quad renders with correct UVs and PointClamp; colour-only meshes byte-identical to today; the vertex-count guard trips loudly (not silently) at the ceiling

Reference implementation: `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj` → `Gmtk2026.Core/MonoDreams/rendering/Component/Draw/DrawComponent.cs` + `System/Draw/MasterRenderSystem.cs`. ⚠️ The MasterRenderSystem file also carries the sort rewrite (#38) and the flip effect (#39) — cherry-pick only the textured branch.

**Value on its own:** one-draw textured geometry for any consumer (terrain chunks, trails, distortion quads), plus a silent web-killing cliff turned into a loud, documented boundary.

1	# rendering — premises
2	
3	> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the rendering pipeline:
4	> `DrawComponent`, `SpriteInfoComponent`, `VisibleComponent`, the
5	> `Camera` class, render targets, `CullingSystem`, `SpritePrepSystem`,
6	> `YSortSystem`, `MasterRenderSystem`, `FinalDrawSystem`, plus the mesh
7	> primitives (`IMeshGenerator`, `MeshData`, `MeshPrepSystem`). Read this
8	> before changing any of those pieces or any system that produces draw
9	> data downstream.
10	
11	## `DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive
12	
13	A `DrawComponent`'s `Type` is one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or
14	`Mesh`. One render component per renderable entity; an entity that needs
15	two visual types needs two entities (or a new `DrawElementType` that
16	composes both).
17	
18	**Why:** `MasterRenderSystem` switches batch context based on `Type`
19	(`Sprite`/`Text`/`NinePatch` go through `SpriteBatch`, `Mesh` goes
20	through `BasicEffect` triangles). Allowing a single `DrawComponent` to
21	span two types would force every render path through a per-call branch.
22	**Breaks:** game code that sets a `DrawComponent` to one type and then
23	expects sprite + text behavior renders only one of them, with no
24	diagnostic.
25	**Tests:** none yet.
26	**Depends on:** —
27	
28	## `DrawComponent` is the only render component
29	
30	Do not create new draw or render components. Adding a new visual type
31	extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork the
32	pipeline.
33	
34	**Why:** a parallel render component would also need a parallel render
35	system, parallel culling treatment, and parallel layer-depth handling —
36	the framework's value comes from there being exactly one path through
37	the pipeline.
38	**Breaks:** the parallel system either skips entities the main path
39	expected (silent invisibility) or competes with it (z-fighting,
40	double-rendering).
41	**Tests:** none yet.
42	**Depends on:** —
43	
44	## `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole render *implementation*
45	
46	All `SpriteBatch` / `BasicEffect` draw calls happen inside
47	`MasterRenderSystem` (back-buffer composition is `FinalDrawSystem`'s job).
48	Game code must not call `SpriteBatch` directly and must not write a second
49	render system. This is about a single *implementation*, not a single
50	*instance*: a screen registers as many `MasterRenderSystem` instances as it
51	has views (see "One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass").
52	
53	**Why:** centralizing the draw call lets one well-understood class own the
54	render-target switch, the batch settings, the sort, and the layer-depth
55	contract. A bespoke second renderer fragments all four; N instances of the
56	*same* renderer do not.
57	**Breaks:** a parallel hand-rolled renderer fights over the active
58	`SpriteBatch`, producing flickering frames, dropped draws, or driver-level
59	errors, and bypasses the sort/layer-depth contract.
60	**Tests:** none yet.
61	**Depends on:** —
62	
63	## One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass
64	
65	A `MasterRenderSystem` instance renders exactly one pass: every entity
66	whose `DrawComponent.Target` equals its `source` id, through its optional
67	`camera` (null ⇒ screen-space, identity transform), into its `destination`
68	render target, which it clears to transparent first. The `source == Main`
69	pass additionally filters on `VisibleComponent` (culling); screen-space
70	passes always render. Multiple cameras, minimaps, splitscreen, CCTV, and
71	portal textures are all just additional instances — a minimap is a second
72	instance with `source = Main`, a second camera, and its own target.
73	`FinalDrawSystem` then composites the targets onto the screen.
74	
75	**Why:** decoupling *what* to draw (`source`), *how* (`camera`), and
76	*where* (`destination`) makes a second view a second instance, not a new
77	code path — the framework's general-over-specialized rule. It also removes
78	the old "the camera only applies to the Main-keyed target" coupling.
79	**Breaks:** two instances writing the *same* destination clear each
80	other's work (each clears on entry) — give every pass its own target and
81	let `FinalDrawSystem` overlap them. Expecting a non-Main source to honor
82	culling: only `source == Main` consults `VisibleComponent`.
83	**Tests:** none yet (the multi-pass + minimap path is exercised by the
84	camera demo, `MonoDreams/camera/demo/CameraDemoScreen.cs`).
85	**Depends on:** "A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its
86	destination".
87	
88	## A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its destination
89	
90	A `MasterRenderSystem` pass derives its mesh `BasicEffect` projection from
91	the *destination* render target's pixel size
92	(`CreateOrthographicOffCenter(0, dest.Width, dest.Height, 0, …)`), and the
93	camera's view transform centers the view at the camera's virtual
94	resolution. For the two to agree, a pass's `camera.VirtualWidth/Height`
95	must equal its destination render target's size. The minimap obeys this by
96	giving its second camera the same virtual resolution as the main camera and
97	a full-virtual-resolution target, then letting `FinalDrawSystem` shrink
98	that target into the on-screen box.
99	
100	**Why:** projection maps destination pixels → NDC; the camera centers world
101	content at `(VirtualWidth/2, VirtualHeight/2)`. A mismatch puts the centered
102	content somewhere other than the target's middle and scales meshes wrongly.
103	Deriving projection from the destination (not the camera) is what lets
104	screen-space passes carry no camera at all.
105	**Breaks:** a camera whose virtual resolution differs from its destination
106	renders off-center and mis-scaled in that pass.
107	**Tests:** none yet.
108	**Depends on:** "`Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable".
109	
110	## `FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list
111	
112	`FinalDrawSystem` takes an ordered `RenderLayer` list and draws each
113	target onto the back buffer in order (later = on top). `RenderLayer.Main`
114	/ `UI` / `HUD` are factories for the standard full-frame layers — all three
115	draw to the aspect-fit `ViewportManager.DestinationRectangle` (with their
116	own samplers), so they share one letterboxed viewport and never stretch or
117	spill into the bars; `RenderLayer.Overlay` places a target in a
118	sub-rectangle given in HUD virtual coordinates, mapped into that same
119	`DestinationRectangle` — so an overlay aligns with HUD chrome drawn at
120	those coordinates; `RenderLayer.Native` composites a provider-resolved
121	target 1:1 over the whole window (native resolution, no aspect-fit — the
122	editor shell's chrome layer), skipping the layer when the provider returns
123	null (how chrome contributes nothing outside Edit). The screen owns the
124	list, so it decides which targets exist, their order, and where each lands.
125	
126	**Why:** the compositor is the natural seam for screen layout — overlays
127	(minimap, CCTV), and eventually tiled splitscreen — without touching the
128	renderer. Driving it from an explicit list (rather than a hardcoded
129	Main→UI→HUD sequence) makes those layouts data, not code forks.
130	**Breaks:** omitting a layer silently drops that target from the screen
131	(its render pass still ran and cleared its target — wasted work, blank
132	result). An overlay rect given in screen pixels instead of HUD virtual
133	coords misaligns with HUD chrome under non-1:1 scaling.
134	**Tests:** none yet (exercised by every demo/example screen and the minimap
135	overlay in the camera demo).
136	**Depends on:** —
137	
138	## The HUD layer is aspect-fit, not screen-stretched (cursor depends on it)
139	
140	The HUD render layer is composited to the aspect-fit
141	`ViewportManager.DestinationRectangle`, exactly like Main and UI — never
142	stretched to the raw back-buffer rectangle `(0,0,ScreenWidth,ScreenHeight)`.
143	HUD-space content is authored in virtual coordinates, and the cursor (a
144	`RenderTargetID.HUD` entity) is positioned by `CursorPositionSystem` via
145	`ViewportManager.ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates`, which inverts the aspect-fit
146	transform. The layer must be drawn back through that *same* transform, or the
147	cursor's render and its position math disagree.
148	
149	**Why:** when the screen aspect ratio differs from the virtual one (any
150	letter/pillarboxed window — common on web, where the back buffer is the whole
151	browser canvas), stretching HUD to the full back buffer scales it
152	non-uniformly (square keycaps render as rectangles) and, because the cursor's
153	*position* is still computed in the aspect-fit space, the rendered cursor
154	drifts from the system pointer — they coincide only at the screen centre and
155	separate toward the edges by the letterbox amount.
156	**Breaks:** giving the HUD layer (or `Overlay`'s `MapVirtualToScreen`) the
157	`(0,0,ScreenWidth,ScreenHeight)` destination instead of `DestinationRectangle`
158	reintroduces the stretch + cursor-drift. At a matching aspect ratio the two
159	rectangles are equal, so the bug is invisible at 16:9 and only appears once the
160	window aspect diverges — test/observe at a non-virtual aspect ratio.
161	**Tests:** none yet (desktop headless renders at the virtual 16:9 resolution,
162	where the rectangles coincide; observed on the web heads at arbitrary window
163	aspects).
164	**Depends on:** —
165	
166	## Renderable entity stack on the Main target
167	
168	An entity is rendered to the Main target only if it has
169	`TransformComponent + SpriteInfoComponent (or text/mesh equivalent) +
170	DrawComponent + VisibleComponent`. Missing `VisibleComponent` means
171	`MasterRenderSystem` skips silently (it includes `.With<VisibleComponent>()`
172	in the Main-target query).
173	
174	**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is the culling output. `CullingSystem` adds
175	it for entities inside the camera frustum and removes it for entities
176	outside, letting `MasterRenderSystem` skip a frustum check per entity.
177	Splitting it from `DrawComponent` is a wart — see Aspirational.
178	**Breaks:** the canonical missed-tag bug — a dev creates an entity with
179	`SpriteInfoComponent + DrawComponent` and stares at an invisible result
180	with no error. Forgetting to register `CullingSystem` in a new screen
181	makes everything Main-target invisible.
182	**Tests:** none yet. *This is the specific bug from the bootstrap
183	interview that motivated writing premises files in the first place.*
184	**Depends on:** "`VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`".
185	
186	## `VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`
187	
188	Game code must not add or remove `VisibleComponent` on Main-target
189	entities. It is managed automatically by `CullingSystem` based on the
190	camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. UI and HUD entities may set
191	`VisibleComponent` themselves as a one-shot tag, since those targets
192	ignore culling (see "Three render targets, two behaviors").
193	
194	**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is a derived state on the Main target. Manual
195	mutation creates ghost entities (visible but outside the frustum, wasting
196	draw calls) or phantom-invisible entities (inside the frustum but
197	skipped). `CullingSystem` will overwrite the game-set value next frame
198	anyway.
199	**Breaks:** entities flicker in and out as `CullingSystem` overwrites
200	game-set values frame to frame; or the cull check fights game code
201	forever.
202	**Tests:** none yet.
203	**Depends on:** —
204	
205	## Three render targets, two behaviors
206	
207	`RenderTargetID.Main` is camera-transformed and respects culling.
208	`RenderTargetID.UI` and `RenderTargetID.HUD` are screen-space and always
209	render. Only Main consults `VisibleComponent`. The later additions follow
210	the screen-space behavior: `RenderTargetID.Scroll` (virtual-space overlay,
211	see its own premise) and `RenderTargetID.Editor` (the editor shell's
212	chrome at **native window resolution**, composited 1:1 by
213	`RenderLayer.Native` — entities on it lay out in physical screen pixels,
214	never virtual coordinates).
215	
216	**Why:** UI and HUD are always-on-screen by definition. Culling them
217	would mean checking against the *screen* frustum, which is a degenerate
218	case (everything is inside). `MasterRenderSystem` enforces this by only
219	adding `.With<VisibleComponent>()` to the Main-target query.
220	**Breaks:** putting a Main-target entity on UI/HUD by mistake skips
221	camera transforms — the entity renders at its world coordinates,
222	unscaled by zoom. The reverse (UI on Main) gets culled away when the
223	camera moves. Authoring Editor-target content in virtual coordinates
224	renders it at the wrong scale/position (the Editor layer is never
225	aspect-fit).
226	**Tests:** none yet.
227	**Depends on:** —
228	
229	## The viewport inset moves compositing and mouse mapping together
230	
231	`ViewportManager.SetViewportInset(left, top, right, bottom)` reserves chrome
232	margins (the editor shell) around the game viewport: the aspect-fit
233	`DestinationRectangle` — and the pixel-perfect rectangle — are computed
234	inside the remaining centered sub-rectangle, and
235	`ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates` inverts that **same** rectangle. Because the
236	`ViewportManager` is the single source of truth, the final-draw compositing
237	and the cursor's virtual/world mapping can never disagree: a click inside the
238	inset viewport maps to the correct virtual point with no extra math, and a
239	click in the margins maps to `null` (`CursorPositionSystem` then flags
240	`CursorInputComponent.OutsideViewport`; chrome consumes the click in screen
241	space). An all-zero inset (the default, and `ClearViewportInset`) is
242	**byte-identical** to the historical full-window letterbox, so every screen
243	that never sets an inset is untouched. `IntegerScale` and
244	`PixelPerfectDestinationRectangle` recalculate lazily like
245	`DestinationRectangle` (a read after a resize/inset change is never stale) —
246	and `Recalculate` must assign their backing fields directly (reading the lazy
247	properties inside it recurses). The same single-source-of-truth rule extends
248	to `DevicePixelRatio` (default 1): when a host renders a device-resolution
249	backbuffer behind a logically-scaled window (macOS Retina under the editor
250	run flag — the level-editor module's `EditorHiDpi`), `ScreenWidth/Height`
251	are DEVICE pixels and `CursorInputSystem` multiplies the raw (logical) mouse
252	by this ratio, so `ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates` keeps inverting the same
253	space it composites in — at DPR 1 everything is byte-identical.
254	
255	**Why:** the Wave-7 editor shell renders the game scaled-down in the center
256	with chrome around it; splitting the inset across two owners (compositor vs
257	mouse mapping) would desync every world pick by the margin offsets — the
258	exact class of bug the aspect-fit HUD premise exists for.
259	**Breaks:** an inset applied to `DestinationRectangle` but not to the mouse
260	inverse shifts all picking by (left, top); a non-restored inset (screen swap
261	without cleanup) letterboxes the next screen into a corner; a stale
262	`PixelPerfectDestinationRectangle` composites the Main layer one
263	resize/inset behind.
264	**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/ViewportInsetTests.cs` (zero-inset =
265	legacy rect + legacy mouse mapping; set+clear restores; inset rect centered
266	and aspect-correct in the available area; mouse maps inside / nulls in the
267	margins; resize recomputes; pixel-perfect uses the available area; negative
268	margins throw; oversized margins clamp).
269	**Depends on:** "The HUD layer is aspect-fit, not screen-stretched (cursor
270	depends on it)"; level-editor — "The editor shell insets the game viewport
271	and renders its chrome at native resolution".
272	
273	## `MasterRenderSystem` samples per draw type: sprites/meshes PointClamp, text LinearClamp
274	
275	`MasterRenderSystem` opens a separate `SpriteBatch` for sprites and for text so each gets
276	its own `SamplerState`. Sprites (and the mesh path) default to `PointClamp` — crisp
277	nearest-neighbour scaling for pixel art; text defaults to `LinearClamp` — smooth filtering
278	for bitmap fonts drawn at fractional scale. Both defaults are overridable via the
279	`spriteSampler` / `textSampler` constructor parameters. Because Sprite and Text are now
280	distinct batch types, the interleaved renderer flushes + reopens the batch when switching
281	between them; painter's order is preserved because the draw list is already depth-sorted.
282	
283	**Why:** a single global `LinearClamp` blurred up-scaled pixel sprites (e.g. a 16×16
284	indicator drawn at 48×48); a single global `PointClamp` aliases down-scaled bitmap text.
285	Per-type samplers give each its correct filtering. The mesh path already forced `PointClamp`
286	(`ResetGraphicsStateForMeshRendering`), so sprites now match it.
287	**Breaks:** collapsing the Sprite/Text batch split (one sampler for both) forces a single
288	filter and reintroduces either blurry sprites or aliased text. Passing a non-clamp address
289	mode would wrap/tile sprites at their edges.
290	**Tests:** none yet.
291	**Depends on:** —
292	
293	## Sprite runs flush below the Reach 16-bit-index budget
294	
295	`MasterRenderSystem` caps the number of sprite quads submitted between a single
296	`SpriteBatch.Begin` and its matching `End`. When a contiguous sprite/text run
297	would push the running quad count past `SpriteBatchFlush.MaxSpritesPerBatch`
298	(a constant strictly below 5461), the renderer flushes (`End` + `Begin`, with
299	the same sampler) and resets the count before drawing the next element. Text
300	elements count one quad per glyph (plus one underline bar per line); a sprite or
301	pre-expanded nine-patch counts one. The cap is applied on **every** graphics
302	profile — the renderer contains no `GraphicsProfile` literal or `#if`.
303	
304	**Why:** MonoGame's / KNI's `SpriteBatch` packs 4 vertices + 6 indices per
305	sprite; once one batch exceeds 5461 sprites it grows to 32-bit indices, which
306	the Reach profile (WebGL ES2 / BlazorGL) rejects with `Reach profile does not
307	support 32 bit indices`. A dense LDtk tile world exceeds 5461 on-screen sprites
308	even after culling, so without the split it paints on desktop (HiDef) but throws
309	on web. Splitting unconditionally keeps the engine source platform-agnostic
310	("the platform is selected by the head") — the head picks Reach vs HiDef; the
311	renderer never asks.
312	**Breaks:** removing the cap, raising it to/past 5461, or counting glyph-heavy
313	text as one quad lets a dense run cross into 32-bit indices and crash a web
314	build; capping too low pointlessly multiplies draw calls.
315	**Residual limitation (one draw call cannot be split):** the split happens
316	*between* draw elements, never *within* one. A single `DrawComponent` whose own
317	`EstimateSpriteQuads` already exceeds the 5461 hard limit — e.g. a >5461-glyph
318	text block on one line — is still submitted in one `SpriteBatch.Draw`/`DrawString`,
319	so it alone crosses into 32-bit indices and throws on Reach. The cap's headroom
320	(4096→5461) absorbs the conservative text over-estimate of a *normal* element,
321	not a pathologically huge one. Splitting one `DrawString` is the framework's job,
322	not the renderer's; if a game legitimately needs a single >5461-glyph run on web,
323	`TextPrepSystem` (rendering-text) must break it into multiple text entities first.
324	This residue is out of the splitter's reach by construction.
325	**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/SpriteBatchFlushTests.cs` — asserts the
326	cap stays below the 32-bit-index hard limit, that a 20000-sprite run splits into
327	segments each within the limit with no quads lost, and that text is counted per
328	glyph. The tests drive the **same** `SpriteBatchFlush.BatchRun` accumulator that
329	`MasterRenderSystem.RenderInterleaved` uses for its per-element flush decision, so
330	a regression inside the renderer's loop (dropping the per-`Begin` reset or skipping
331	the flush check) is reflected in the unit test, not only in an on-device web run.
332	The desktop demo headless tests
333	(`MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`) confirm the split is
334	visually transparent on HiDef.
335	**Depends on:** foundation — "The platform … is selected by the head project,
336	never by engine source".
337	
338	## Mesh indices render through 16-bit indices (Reach-safe)
339	
340	`MasterRenderSystem.DrawSingleMesh` draws a mesh through the **`short[]`** overload of
341	`GraphicsDevice.DrawUserIndexedPrimitives`, using the 16-bit index array
342	`DrawComponent.Get16BitIndices()` returns. Meshes are authored with `int[]` indices
343	(`MeshData.Indices`, every `IMeshGenerator`), so `Get16BitIndices()` converts once and caches
344	the result, rebuilding only when `Indices` is reassigned (reference identity changes). It
345	returns `null` only when the mesh has more vertices than a 16-bit index can address (more than
346	65536); the renderer then falls back to the 32-bit `int[]` overload, which is valid only on
347	HiDef. As with the sprite-run flush, the renderer contains no `GraphicsProfile` literal — the
348	16-bit path is taken on every profile.
349	
350	**Why:** the overload's index-array type selects the GPU index width (`int[]` ⇒ 32-bit,
351	`short[]` ⇒ 16-bit), and the Reach profile (WebGL ES2 / BlazorGL) rejects 32-bit indices with
352	`Reach profile does not support 32 bit indices`. The player's orb is a `CircleMeshGenerator`
353	mesh; before this, its `int[]` indices took the 32-bit overload and threw on the first web
354	render tick (it painted on desktop, where HiDef accepts 32-bit). This is the mesh analog of the
355	sprite-run flush — both keep mesh/sprite submissions inside the 16-bit budget so the engine
356	source stays platform-agnostic.
357	**Breaks:** rendering meshes through the `int[]` overload again (e.g. passing `dc.Indices`
358	directly) reintroduces the Reach crash for every mesh-backed entity — orbs, the demo UI
359	buttons/checkboxes, physics-demo circles. Converting per frame instead of caching reintroduces
360	a per-frame allocation that fails the headless heap-flat assertion.
361	**Caching note:** the cache keys off the `Indices` array reference, not `SetMeshData` — factories
362	that set `DrawComponent.Indices` directly (e.g. `PlayerEntityFactory`) still get a correct,
363	rebuilt-on-change conversion.
364	**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/MeshIndexConversionTests.cs` — asserts the short values
365	match the int indices, that the conversion is cached across calls and rebuilt on reassignment,
366	that values above 32767 round-trip as unsigned 16-bit bit patterns, and that a mesh past the
367	16-bit vertex ceiling returns `null` (32-bit fallback). The physics/UI demo headless tests
368	exercise the mesh path on HiDef; the in-browser physics demo confirms it on Reach.
369	**Depends on:** foundation — "The platform … is selected by the head project,
370	never by engine source".
371	
372	## The draw set is built once per instance, not per frame
373	
374	A `MasterRenderSystem` instance builds its `EntitySet` (for its `source`)
375	lazily once and reuses it for the instance's lifetime; it is disposed in
376	`Dispose`. It must never call `world.GetEntities()...AsSet()` inside the
377	per-frame `Update`.
378	
379	**Why:** DefaultEcs's `AsSet()` registers component/entity lifecycle
380	subscriptions on the `World`, and the World holds those subscription
381	delegates — which reference the `EntitySet` — alive forever. A set
382	created per frame is therefore never garbage-collected. An earlier version
383	built a fresh set every frame, leaking `EntitySet`s every frame, each
384	retaining its matched-entity array. This is the standing ECS-wide rule
385	(every other `AsSet()` in the engine is cached in a field) applied to the
386	renderer. Note that composing N render passes means N cached sets — fine,
387	because each is built once; two passes with the same `source` (e.g. the
388	main world pass and a minimap pass) hold two equivalent sets, a negligible
389	constant cost, not a per-frame leak.
390	**Breaks:** process memory climbs steadily even on a fully static scene
391	(no entities or assets added), as observed in the camera and physics
392	demos. Eventually OOM on a long-running session.
393	**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`
394	asserts a flat live heap across 600 frames of the camera demo (now four
395	render passes).
396	**Depends on:** —
397	
398	## Rendering systems run last in the pipeline
399	
400	In any screen's pipeline assembly, the prep / cull / sort / render stage
401	goes at the tail. Logic that mutates renderable state (positions, sprite
402	source rects, text contents, layer depths) must complete before the prep
403	module reads it.
404	
405	**Why:** the prep stage freezes the state of `DrawComponent`s into the
406	draw queue; mutations after the queue is built are silently lost until
407	next frame.
408	**Breaks:** a game system that updates text mid-render-module sees the
409	old text on screen. A movement system after `CullingSystem` updates
410	positions without re-culling — entities pop in or out by one frame.
411	**Tests:** none yet.
412	**Depends on:** —
413	
414	## Layer-depth ownership pipeline
415	
416	`SpritePrepSystem` initializes `DrawComponent.LayerDepth` from
417	`SpriteInfoComponent.LayerDepth`. `YSortSystem` may override it for
418	entities on Y-sorted layers. `MasterRenderSystem` sorts on the final
419	value. Game systems writing `LayerDepth` after `YSortSystem` create
420	undefined sort behavior.
421	
422	**Why:** three writers in a defined order produce one final value. A
423	fourth writer in between (or after) breaks the contract.
424	**Breaks:** entities flicker, depth-fight, or render behind/in-front of
425	static elements unexpectedly.
426	**Tests:** none yet.
427	**Depends on:** —
428	
429	## A sprite's drawn quad honors `Transform.WorldScale` exactly once
430	
431	`MasterRenderSystem`'s Sprite draw scale is `(DrawComponent.Size / SourceRectangle) ·
432	DrawComponent.Scale` (`MasterRenderSystem.ComputeSpriteScale`). `SpritePrepSystem` writes
433	`DrawComponent.Size = SpriteInfoComponent.Size` (the SOURCE size) and `DrawComponent.Scale =
434	Transform.WorldScale` as **two separate fields — `WorldScale` is never pre-baked into `Size`**.
435	Composing the two (not discarding `Scale` whenever a source rect exists, which was the bug) is what
436	makes a world-scaled sprite's drawn quad equal the quad `GizmoTransform.SpriteWorldQuad` hit-tests —
437	the selection outline, picking and collider proxies all use that same `WorldScale · (Size / source)`
438	product. With **no** source rectangle the raw `Scale` applies (the nine-patch / pre-sized-texture
439	path, untouched). Because `DrawComponent.Scale` defaults to `Vector2.One` and only `SpritePrepSystem`
440	ever writes a non-unit value, the composition is **byte-identical** to the pre-fix `Size / source` for
441	every unscaled sprite — including entities that set `Size` deliberately and never touch `Scale` (the
442	palette thumbnail on the Editor target; the textured cursor), so they never double-scale.
443	
444	**Why:** a gizmo scale-drag mutates `Transform.Scale`; before the fix the outline and colliders
445	(transform math) grew but the sprite — whose draw scale discarded `Scale` in the source-rect branch —
446	did not (the user-reported "scaling grows the box but not the art" bug). The one invariant: the drawn
447	quad and the hit-test quad are the SAME quad, so what you grab is what you see. **Audit (the fix's
448	mandatory pre-mortem — does any writer pre-bake `WorldScale` into `Size`?):** no. Every
449	`DrawComponent.Size` writer — `SpritePrepSystem`, `SceneReaderSystem.RestoreDrawComponents` (bare,
450	`Size` unset → `SpritePrepSystem` fills it next frame), the palette ghost (via
451	`SpriteInfoComponent.Size` → `SpritePrepSystem`), the palette thumbnail, the textured cursor — sets
452	`Size` to a source/destination pixel size independent of the transform scale, so composing multiplies
453	the world scale in exactly once.
454	**Breaks:** discarding `Scale` in the source-rect branch (the pre-fix behavior) leaves every placed
455	prop un-scalable — outline and sprite diverge. Pre-baking `WorldScale` into any `Size` writer AND
456	composing multiplies it twice (the sprite grows quadratically per drag). A thumbnail/cursor path that
457	sets both a non-unit `Scale` and a deliberate `Size` double-scales.
458	**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/SpriteDrawScaleTests.cs` (a 2×3 world-scaled source-rect
459	sprite's drawn quad matches `SpriteWorldQuad`; unit scale is byte-identical to the old `Size /
460	source`; a deliberate-`Size` unit-`Scale` sprite — the thumbnail/cursor path — does not double-scale;
461	no source rect uses the raw `Scale`).
462	**Depends on:** "Layer-depth ownership pipeline" (`SpritePrepSystem` populates `DrawComponent` from
463	`SpriteInfoComponent` + the transform each frame); level-editor — "The gizmo applies a quantized
464	(snap-on) or raw (snap-off) transform edit, honoring Origin" (the `WorldScale` edit whose visual this
465	reflects) and "Y-sorted props use the feet-origin convention, factory-applied"
466	(`SpriteWorldQuad`'s Size/source/origin inputs).
467	
468	## Sprite facing/orientation is a flip flag, not mirrored art
469	
470	A sprite's facing/orientation is expressed by `SpriteInfoComponent.FlipHorizontally` /
471	`FlipVertically`, copied by `SpritePrepSystem` into `DrawComponent` (both branches — regular sprite
472	and nine-patch) and applied by `MasterRenderSystem` as OR-combined `SpriteEffects`
473	(`MasterRenderSystem.ComputeSpriteEffects`) — the GPU mirrors the quad for free. No sprite sheet
474	should bake a mirrored row/column just to get the other facing. The flip mirrors pixels INSIDE the
475	destination rect: `Origin` semantics are unchanged (still measured from the source's top-left), the
476	drawn quad equals the unflipped quad, so hit-testing / gizmo quads
477	(`GizmoTransform.SpriteWorldQuad`) are unaffected, and flips compose freely with rotation, scale and
478	non-centred origins. Both flags default `false`, and `ComputeSpriteEffects` composes those defaults
479	to `SpriteEffects.None`, so existing content renders byte-identical. Shear/skew is explicitly NOT a
480	flag: `SpriteBatch` has no per-sprite shear (it would need a batch-wide `transformMatrix` or
481	arbitrary vertices), so skew belongs to the textured-mesh path — do not go looking for a shear flag
482	on this seam. The scene serializer persists the flags **omit-when-false**, so pre-flip `.mdscene`
483	files stay byte-identical.
484	
485	**Why:** every directional thing in a 2D game (walkers, projectiles, corpses, tumbling pickups)
486	otherwise needs double art; with the flags the seam now exposes everything `SpriteBatch` can do
487	per-draw.
488	**Breaks:** baking mirrored rows wastes sheet space and desyncs the two facings as animations are
489	added; a game system writing `SpriteEffects` anywhere else would fork the seam; serializing the flags
490	unconditionally would break the committed-scene byte fixed point.
491	**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/SpriteFlipTests.cs` (all four `ComputeSpriteEffects`
492	combinations, the byte-identical `None` default, fresh `SpriteInfoComponent` / `DrawComponent`
493	defaults, `SpritePrepSystem` copying both flags without perturbing the transform fields, and the
494	serializer round-trip: flags round-trip true, a default sprite writes neither key, an absent key
495	reads false).
496	**Depends on:** "A sprite's drawn quad honors `Transform.WorldScale` exactly once" (the same
497	drawn-quad-equals-hit-test-quad invariant this must not disturb); level-editor — "Scene
498	serialization is canonical and byte-stable; `entities[]` is ordered by a persisted stable scene-local
499	id" and "`SpriteInfoComponent` serializes an `AssetKey`, never the live `Texture2D`".
500	
501	## Y-sort tiebreaker is parent-child bias only
502	
503	`YSortSystem` uses a minimal epsilon (`1e-6f` in
504	`MonoDreams/rendering/System/Draw/YSortSystem.cs`) to bias children
505	relative to their parent's final depth, preserving group ordering.
506	Same-layer entities at the same world Y with no parent-child relationship
507	have no further tiebreaker — render order falls through to entity
508	insertion order.
509	
510	**Why:** parent-child bias is the only ambiguity case the framework
511	treats explicitly; "true ties" are rare in practice (entities at the
512	exact same Y on the same layer).
513	**Breaks:** if true ties become common, flicker can appear when
514	insertion order changes (e.g., re-spawn). The fix is a tiebreaker —
515	possibly entity ID — but that's a framework change, not a workaround.
516	**Tests:** none yet.
517	**Depends on:** —
518	
519	## `Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable; the `Camera` is a render adapter (CM)
520	
521	`Camera.VirtualWidth` and `Camera.VirtualHeight` are readonly properties
522	set in the constructor (the `Camera` class lives at
523	`MonoDreams/rendering/Camera.cs` because it is a hard dependency of the
524	draw stack — `MasterRenderSystem` reads its position, zoom, and view
525	matrix every frame). Only zoom, position, and rotation are mutable on a
526	live `Camera`.
527	
528	**Under CM the `Camera` is a render ADAPTER, and rendering is unchanged.** The
529	authored camera is a scene ENTITY (`camera` module — `CameraComponent` + the
530	entity's `TransformComponent`); `CameraSyncSystem` copies that entity's pose
531	into this `Camera` each frame in Play. The draw stack still consumes a plain
532	`Camera` exactly as before — the `Camera` class, its mutable
533	position/zoom/rotation, and the immutable virtual resolution are all UNCHANGED.
534	The camera-as-entity model added zero rendering-module code; it only changed
535	*who writes* the adapter (a `camera`-module system, not game code or a
536	`scene.camera` file block).
537	
538	**Why:** virtual resolution defines the world-units-per-pixel ratio.
539	Changing it mid-frame would require recomputing every entity's on-screen
540	size and re-running culling. Keeping the `Camera` a plain adapter is what let CM
541	demote it without touching the render path.
542	**Breaks:** a system that tries to change resolution at runtime either
543	silently fails (readonly) or, if it bypasses, produces a fractional
544	frame where culling, layout, and rendering disagree. Moving the virtual
545	resolution onto the camera *entity* (scene data) would couple the file to an
546	immutable render setting.
547	**Tests:** none yet (the adapter-write path is `camera` — "`CameraSyncSystem` is
548	the only writer of the `Camera` adapter in Play").
549	**Depends on:** camera — "`CameraSyncSystem` is the only writer of the `Camera`
550	adapter in Play".
551	
552	## `IMeshGenerator.Generate()` returns a triangle list
553	
554	All canonical generators (`CircleMeshGenerator`, `CircleOutlineMeshGenerator`,
555	`LineMeshGenerator`, `RectangleOutlineMeshGenerator`,
556	`RoundedRectangleOutlineMeshGenerator`,
557	`DashedRectangleOutlineMeshGenerator`, `FilledRectangleMeshGenerator`,
558	`FilledRoundedRectangleMeshGenerator`, `FilledTriangleMeshGenerator`,
559	`FilledPolygonMeshGenerator`, `PolygonOutlineMeshGenerator`,
560	`PolylineMeshGenerator`, `GradientPathMeshGenerator`,
561	`CompositeMeshGenerator`) return `MeshData`
562	whose indices describe a triangle list — every triple of indices is one
563	triangle. `MasterRenderSystem` invokes `DrawUserIndexedPrimitives` with
564	`PrimitiveType.TriangleList`. The filled triangle/polygon generators rely on
565	the mesh path's `CullNone` rasterizer state, so their winding order is free.
566	
567	**Why:** triangle lists are the lowest common denominator for the
568	`BasicEffect` path. Triangle strips or fans would require per-shape
569	metadata about which primitive type to use, and would multiply the
570	render path's branching.
571	**Breaks:** a custom generator that emits a triangle strip without
572	setting `DrawComponent.PrimitiveType` correctly produces garbled
573	geometry — the renderer interprets the indices as a list and draws
574	random triangles between them.
575	**Tests:** none yet.
576	**Depends on:** —
577	
578	## `MeshPrepSystem` writes the world matrix once per frame
579	
580	`MeshPrepSystem` reads `TransformComponent.WorldMatrix` and writes it
581	into `DrawComponent.WorldMatrix` for every entity with `Type = Mesh`.
582	This must happen after `HierarchySystem` propagates dirty flags and
583	before `MasterRenderSystem` reads the matrix to bind it to
584	`BasicEffect.World`.
585	
586	**Why:** meshes render in world space — their vertex positions are
587	the geometry's local-space layout, and the world matrix transforms
588	them to where the entity is. Reading `TransformComponent.WorldMatrix`
589	in `MasterRenderSystem` directly would couple the renderer to the
590	transform; staging through `DrawComponent` keeps the renderer
591	agnostic.
592	**Breaks:** running `MeshPrepSystem` before `HierarchySystem` produces
593	meshes positioned by last frame's parent transform (one-frame lag on
594	parented meshes). Running it after `MasterRenderSystem` is too late —
595	the renderer uses the previous frame's world matrix.
596	**Tests:** none yet.
597	**Depends on:** foundation — "`HierarchySystem` must run ahead of any
598	system reading WorldPosition"; "Rendering systems run last in the
599	pipeline" (above).
600	
601	## `CompositeMeshGenerator` rebases indices into the combined buffer
602	
603	When `CompositeMeshGenerator.Generate()` walks its sub-generators, it
604	adds each sub-mesh's vertices to a combined vertex list and adds
605	`indexOffset` to each sub-mesh's indices before appending to the
606	combined index list. A sub-generator returning indices that already
607	reference the combined buffer's range would draw the wrong triangles.
608	
609	**Why:** composability is the design goal — a button outline + label
610	backdrop + glow can be one mesh entity. The rebase invariant is what
611	makes "just add another generator" work without per-generator
612	coordination.
613	**Breaks:** a custom generator that returns indices unrelated to its
614	own vertex buffer (e.g. via a stale cached array) corrupts the
615	composite's geometry. The bug manifests as visible triangles between
616	unrelated parts of the composite.
617	**Tests:** none yet.
618	**Depends on:** —
619	
620	## The mesh render path uses premultiplied alpha — UI fills must be opaque
621	
622	The mesh path (`DrawComponent.Type = Mesh`, rendered through `BasicEffect`
623	triangles in `MasterRenderSystem`) draws into render targets that composite
624	with **premultiplied alpha**. The vertex colors in `MeshData` are *not*
625	premultiplied by the generators, so a fill color with partial alpha
626	(`A` in `1..254`) renders far brighter than a designer expects — the
627	straight-alpha RGB is composited as if it were already premultiplied, so
628	a 50%-alpha mid-grey reads as near-white. UI mesh fills must therefore be
629	**opaque** (`A == 255`). Fully transparent (`A == 0`, `Color.Transparent`)
630	is also safe because the prep/draw path skips a zero-alpha fill entirely
631	(`ButtonMeshPrepSystem` produces a degenerate mesh; `ToggleSwitchSystem`
632	empties the mesh) — that's how a "no fill" button or an "off" checkbox is
633	expressed. Encode translucency by choosing a darker opaque color, not by
634	lowering alpha.
635	
636	**Why:** the targets blend premultiplied; matching that would mean
637	premultiplying every vertex color in the generators or the prep systems,
638	which nothing does today. Restricting UI fills to opaque (or fully
639	transparent) sidesteps the brightness blow-up without a pipeline-wide color
640	transform. `ButtonTheme` / `ButtonVariantColors` pick opaque fills for this
641	reason, and `ButtonVisualSystem` keys the "no fill" state off `A == 0`.
642	**Breaks:** a button or panel given a partial-alpha fill (e.g. a "subtle"
643	`Color.Black * 0.3f`) renders as a glaring near-white block instead of a
644	faint tint — the canonical "why is my overlay white?" bug. Lowering alpha
645	to dim a fill makes it brighter, not dimmer.
646	**Tests:** none yet (exercised by every demo with mesh-backed UI — the
647	`ui` demo's buttons / panels, the camera and physics demos' checkboxes).
648	**Depends on:** "`IMeshGenerator.Generate()` returns a triangle list";
649	ui — "`ToggleSwitchComponent` drives a checkmark mesh's visibility from a
650	bool".
651	
652	## Scrollable content uses a dedicated `RenderTargetID.Scroll` target composited via `RenderLayer.Overlay`
653	
654	Scrollable UI regions render into their own `RenderTargetID.Scroll` render
655	target, composited onto the screen by a `RenderLayer.Overlay` entry in
656	`FinalDrawSystem`'s layer list. The overlay's HUD-virtual sub-rectangle is
657	the scroll viewport, so content drawn past the target's edges is clipped by
658	the target bounds (the overlay maps the whole target into the viewport box —
659	content outside the box's mapped region does not appear). Like UI and HUD,
660	the `Scroll` target is screen-space and always renders regardless of
661	`VisibleComponent`. For now there is **one** `Scroll` region per screen: a
662	screen registers a single `source = Scroll` `MasterRenderSystem` pass and a
663	single overlay layer for it.
664	
665	**Why:** clipping a sub-region of scrolling content is exactly what a
666	separate render target plus an overlay sub-rect gives for free — the target
667	is the clip rect, the overlay is the placement. Reusing the existing
668	multi-pass + `RenderLayer.Overlay` machinery (the same path the minimap
669	uses) keeps scrolling as data, not a new code path. Bounding it to one
670	region per screen avoids inventing per-region target allocation before a
671	second region is actually needed.
672	**Breaks:** drawing scrollable content directly on UI/HUD with no dedicated
673	target gives no clip rect — content spills past the intended viewport.
674	Registering two `Scroll` regions today collides on the single target
675	(each pass clears it on entry, per "One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one
676	render pass"), so the second region erases the first.
677	**Tests:** none yet (exercised by the `ui` demo's scroll region).
678	**Depends on:** "One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass";
679	"`FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list"; "Three
680	render targets, two behaviors".
681	
682	## `RoundedRectangleOutlineMeshGenerator` draws a stroked rounded-rectangle border
683	
684	`RoundedRectangleOutlineMeshGenerator` emits a triangle-list `MeshData` for
685	the *border* of a rounded rectangle (straight edges + quarter-circle corner
686	arcs of a given corner radius, stroked at a given line thickness) — the
687	hollow counterpart to `FilledRoundedRectangleMeshGenerator`'s solid fill. A
688	bordered rounded panel is therefore two sibling mesh entities sharing a
689	`TransformComponent`: a `FilledRoundedRectangleMeshGenerator` fill behind a
690	`RoundedRectangleOutlineMeshGenerator` stroke, exactly as a plain panel pairs
691	`FilledRectangleMeshGenerator` with `RectangleOutlineMeshGenerator`. Both the
692	fill and the outline obey the opaque-fill rule for the mesh path.
693	
694	**Why:** rounded panels and rounded buttons want a crisp border distinct
695	from the fill, and (per `DrawComponent.Type` being mutually exclusive) one
696	mesh entity can carry either the fill *or* the outline, not both — so the
697	border is its own generator on its own entity. Matching the fill generator's
698	corner-radius parameterization lets the two line up pixel-for-pixel.
699	**Breaks:** mismatched corner radii between the fill and the outline leave
700	the stroke floating off the fill's rounded corners. Putting a partial-alpha
701	color on the stroke triggers the premultiplied-alpha brightness bug above.
702	**Tests:** none yet (exercised by the `ui` demo's rounded panels/buttons).
703	**Depends on:** "`IMeshGenerator.Generate()` returns a triangle list";
704	"`DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive"; "The mesh render path uses
705	premultiplied alpha — UI fills must be opaque".
706	
707	## Open questions
708	
709	- **Same-Y flicker in practice** — has this surfaced? If so, the
710	  tiebreaker premise above needs to harden.
711	- **Mixed render targets per entity** — is it ever valid for the same
712	  entity to render on Main *and* HUD (via two separate `DrawComponent`s
713	  on different entities)? Probably always two entities, but not yet a
714	  settled convention.
715	- **`DrawElement` cache invalidation** — what happens if a prep system
716	  mutates `SpriteInfoComponent` after the draw queue was built?
717	- **Texturing meshes** — `MeshData` carries `VertexPositionColor`
718	  vertices; there's no `VertexPositionTexture` path. Whether to add one
719	  (and how it interacts with the SpriteBatch-based sprite path) is open.
720	- **Mesh culling extents** — meshes get `VisibleComponent` from
721	  `CullingSystem` based on `TransformComponent.WorldPosition` against
722	  the camera bounds. A mesh's actual extents (computed from its
723	  vertices) might lie outside the position's frustum, causing visible
724	  pop-out at edges. No bounding-box-from-vertices logic exists today.
725	
726	## Aspirational direction
727	
728	- `VisibleComponent` becomes a property of `DrawComponent` (removes the
729	  easy-to-miss tag).
730	- Multi-view (minimap / splitscreen / CCTV / portals) is now possible by
731	  composing `MasterRenderSystem` instances + `RenderLayer`s (the camera
732	  demo ships a minimap). What's still missing is **per-view culling**: a
733	  `source = Main` pass inherits the main camera's `VisibleComponent`, so a
734	  second camera can't yet cull to *its own* frustum. A per-camera cull set
735	  (or a cull-independent draw set option) is the next step.
736	- Render targets become more configurable — custom post-processing
737	  passes, shader effects.
738	- A `MeshTransformBatcher` that combines static meshes sharing a layer
739	  depth into a single submission, cutting `BasicEffect` draw calls.
740	- Per-vertex texture-coordinate support so meshes can sample sprite
741	  atlases (would let the dialogue indicator or UI nine-patches be a
742	  mesh rather than a `SpriteBatch` ninepatch).
743	
744	## Follow-up debt
745	
746	The following premises currently have **Tests: none yet**:
747	
748	- `DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive
749	- `DrawComponent` is the only render component
750	- `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole render *implementation*
751	- One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass
752	- A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its destination
753	- `FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list
754	- Renderable entity stack on the Main target
755	- `VisibleComponent` is owned exclusively by `CullingSystem`
756	- Three render targets, two behaviors
757	- `MasterRenderSystem` samples per draw type: sprites/meshes PointClamp, text LinearClamp
758	- Rendering systems run last in the pipeline
759	- Layer-depth ownership pipeline
760	- Y-sort tiebreaker is parent-child bias only
761	- `Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable
762	- `IMeshGenerator.Generate()` returns a triangle list
763	- `MeshPrepSystem` writes the world matrix once per frame
764	- `CompositeMeshGenerator` rebases indices into the combined buffer
765	- The mesh render path uses premultiplied alpha — UI fills must be opaque
766	- Scrollable content uses a dedicated `RenderTargetID.Scroll` target composited via `RenderLayer.Overlay`
767	- `RoundedRectangleOutlineMeshGenerator` draws a stroked rounded-rectangle border
768	
769	Architectural tests for ECS-purity premises (no parallel render systems,
770	no game `SpriteBatch` calls, `VisibleComponent` not added outside
771	`CullingSystem` on Main-target entities) are the highest-leverage
772	candidates here.

# rendering — premises

> Technical invariants the engine assumes about the rendering pipeline:
> `DrawComponent`, `SpriteInfoComponent`, `VisibleComponent`, the
> `Camera` class, render targets, `CullingSystem`, `SpritePrepSystem`,
> `YSortSystem`, `MasterRenderSystem`, `FinalDrawSystem`, plus the mesh
> primitives (`IMeshGenerator`, `MeshData`, `MeshPrepSystem`). Read this
> before changing any of those pieces or any system that produces draw
> data downstream.

## `DrawComponent.Type` is mutually exclusive

A `DrawComponent`'s `Type` is one of `Sprite`, `Text`, `NinePatch`, or
`Mesh`. One render component per renderable entity; an entity that needs
two visual types needs two entities (or a new `DrawElementType` that
composes both).

**Why:** `MasterRenderSystem` switches batch context based on `Type`
(`Sprite`/`Text`/`NinePatch` go through `SpriteBatch`, `Mesh` goes
through `BasicEffect` triangles). Allowing a single `DrawComponent` to
span two types would force every render path through a per-call branch.
**Breaks:** game code that sets a `DrawComponent` to one type and then
expects sprite + text behavior renders only one of them, with no
diagnostic.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## `DrawComponent` is the only render component

Do not create new draw or render components. Adding a new visual type
extends `DrawElementType` and `MasterRenderSystem`; it does not fork the
pipeline.

**Why:** a parallel render component would also need a parallel render
system, parallel culling treatment, and parallel layer-depth handling —
the framework's value comes from there being exactly one path through
the pipeline.
**Breaks:** the parallel system either skips entities the main path
expected (silent invisibility) or competes with it (z-fighting,
double-rendering).
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## `MasterRenderSystem` is the sole render *implementation*

All `SpriteBatch` / `BasicEffect` draw calls happen inside
`MasterRenderSystem` (back-buffer composition is `FinalDrawSystem`'s job).
Game code must not call `SpriteBatch` directly and must not write a second
render system. This is about a single *implementation*, not a single
*instance*: a screen registers as many `MasterRenderSystem` instances as it
has views (see "One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass").

**Why:** centralizing the draw call lets one well-understood class own the
render-target switch, the batch settings, the sort, and the layer-depth
contract. A bespoke second renderer fragments all four; N instances of the
*same* renderer do not.
**Breaks:** a parallel hand-rolled renderer fights over the active
`SpriteBatch`, producing flickering frames, dropped draws, or driver-level
errors, and bypasses the sort/layer-depth contract.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## One `MasterRenderSystem` instance is one render pass

A `MasterRenderSystem` instance renders exactly one pass: every entity
whose `DrawComponent.Target` equals its `source` id, through its optional
`camera` (null ⇒ screen-space, identity transform), into its `destination`
render target, which it clears to transparent first. The `source == Main`
pass additionally filters on `VisibleComponent` (culling); screen-space
passes always render. Multiple cameras, minimaps, splitscreen, CCTV, and
portal textures are all just additional instances — a minimap is a second
instance with `source = Main`, a second camera, and its own target.
`FinalDrawSystem` then composites the targets onto the screen.

**Why:** decoupling *what* to draw (`source`), *how* (`camera`), and
*where* (`destination`) makes a second view a second instance, not a new
code path — the framework's general-over-specialized rule. It also removes
the old "the camera only applies to the Main-keyed target" coupling.
**Breaks:** two instances writing the *same* destination clear each
other's work (each clears on entry) — give every pass its own target and
let `FinalDrawSystem` overlap them. Expecting a non-Main source to honor
culling: only `source == Main` consults `VisibleComponent`.
**Tests:** none yet (the multi-pass + minimap path is exercised by the
camera demo, `MonoDreams/camera/demo/CameraDemoScreen.cs`).
**Depends on:** "A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its
destination".

## A render pass's camera virtual resolution matches its destination

A `MasterRenderSystem` pass derives its mesh `BasicEffect` projection from
the *destination* render target's pixel size
(`CreateOrthographicOffCenter(0, dest.Width, dest.Height, 0, …)`), and the
camera's view transform centers the view at the camera's virtual
resolution. For the two to agree, a pass's `camera.VirtualWidth/Height`
must equal its destination render target's size. The minimap obeys this by
giving its second camera the same virtual resolution as the main camera and
a full-virtual-resolution target, then letting `FinalDrawSystem` shrink
that target into the on-screen box.

**Why:** projection maps destination pixels → NDC; the camera centers world
content at `(VirtualWidth/2, VirtualHeight/2)`. A mismatch puts the centered
content somewhere other than the target's middle and scales meshes wrongly.
Deriving projection from the destination (not the camera) is what lets
screen-space passes carry no camera at all.
**Breaks:** a camera whose virtual resolution differs from its destination
renders off-center and mis-scaled in that pass.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** "`Camera.VirtualResolution` is immutable".

## `FinalDrawSystem` composites an explicit, ordered layer list

`FinalDrawSystem` takes an ordered `RenderLayer` list and draws each
target onto the back buffer in order (later = on top). `RenderLayer.Main`
/ `UI` / `HUD` are factories for the standard full-frame layers — all three
draw to the aspect-fit `ViewportManager.DestinationRectangle` (with their
own samplers), so they share one letterboxed viewport and never stretch or
spill into the bars; `RenderLayer.Overlay` places a target in a
sub-rectangle given in HUD virtual coordinates, mapped into that same
`DestinationRectangle` — so an overlay aligns with HUD chrome drawn at
those coordinates; `RenderLayer.Native` composites a provider-resolved
target 1:1 over the whole window (native resolution, no aspect-fit — the
editor shell's chrome layer), skipping the layer when the provider returns
null (how chrome contributes nothing outside Edit). The screen owns the
list, so it decides which targets exist, their order, and where each lands.

**Why:** the compositor is the natural seam for screen layout — overlays
(minimap, CCTV), and eventually tiled splitscreen — without touching the
renderer. Driving it from an explicit list (rather than a hardcoded
Main→UI→HUD sequence) makes those layouts data, not code forks.
**Breaks:** omitting a layer silently drops that target from the screen
(its render pass still ran and cleared its target — wasted work, blank
result). An overlay rect given in screen pixels instead of HUD virtual
coords misaligns with HUD chrome under non-1:1 scaling.
**Tests:** none yet (exercised by every demo/example screen and the minimap
overlay in the camera demo).
**Depends on:** —

## The HUD layer is aspect-fit, not screen-stretched (cursor depends on it)

The HUD render layer is composited to the aspect-fit
`ViewportManager.DestinationRectangle`, exactly like Main and UI — never
stretched to the raw back-buffer rectangle `(0,0,ScreenWidth,ScreenHeight)`.
HUD-space content is authored in virtual coordinates, and the cursor (a
`RenderTargetID.HUD` entity) is positioned by `CursorPositionSystem` via
`ViewportManager.ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates`, which inverts the aspect-fit
transform. The layer must be drawn back through that *same* transform, or the
cursor's render and its position math disagree.

**Why:** when the screen aspect ratio differs from the virtual one (any
letter/pillarboxed window — common on web, where the back buffer is the whole
browser canvas), stretching HUD to the full back buffer scales it
non-uniformly (square keycaps render as rectangles) and, because the cursor's
*position* is still computed in the aspect-fit space, the rendered cursor
drifts from the system pointer — they coincide only at the screen centre and
separate toward the edges by the letterbox amount.
**Breaks:** giving the HUD layer (or `Overlay`'s `MapVirtualToScreen`) the
`(0,0,ScreenWidth,ScreenHeight)` destination instead of `DestinationRectangle`
reintroduces the stretch + cursor-drift. At a matching aspect ratio the two
rectangles are equal, so the bug is invisible at 16:9 and only appears once the
window aspect diverges — test/observe at a non-virtual aspect ratio.
**Tests:** none yet (desktop headless renders at the virtual 16:9 resolution,
where the rectangles coincide; observed on the web heads at arbitrary window
aspects).

DrawComponent + VisibleComponent`. Missing `VisibleComponent` means
`MasterRenderSystem` skips silently (it includes `.With<VisibleComponent>()`
in the Main-target query).

**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is the culling output. `CullingSystem` adds
it for entities inside the camera frustum and removes it for entities
outside, letting `MasterRenderSystem` skip a frustum check per entity.
Splitting it from `DrawComponent` is a wart — see Aspirational.
**Breaks:** the canonical missed-tag bug — a dev creates an entity with
`SpriteInfoComponent + DrawComponent` and stares at an invisible result

Game code must not add or remove `VisibleComponent` on Main-target
entities. It is managed automatically by `CullingSystem` based on the
camera's `VirtualScreenBounds`. UI and HUD entities may set
`VisibleComponent` themselves as a one-shot tag, since those targets
ignore culling (see "Three render targets, two behaviors").

**Why:** `VisibleComponent` is a derived state on the Main target. Manual
mutation creates ghost entities (visible but outside the frustum, wasting
draw calls) or phantom-invisible entities (inside the frustum but
skipped). `CullingSystem` will overwrite the game-set value next frame
anyway.

## Three render targets, two behaviors

`RenderTargetID.Main` is camera-transformed and respects culling.
`RenderTargetID.UI` and `RenderTargetID.HUD` are screen-space and always
render. Only Main consults `VisibleComponent`. The later additions follow
the screen-space behavior: `RenderTargetID.Scroll` (virtual-space overlay,
see its own premise) and `RenderTargetID.Editor` (the editor shell's
chrome at **native window resolution**, composited 1:1 by
`RenderLayer.Native` — entities on it lay out in physical screen pixels,
never virtual coordinates).

**Why:** UI and HUD are always-on-screen by definition. Culling them
would mean checking against the *screen* frustum, which is a degenerate
case (everything is inside). `MasterRenderSystem` enforces this by only
adding `.With<VisibleComponent>()` to the Main-target query.
**Breaks:** putting a Main-target entity on UI/HUD by mistake skips
camera transforms — the entity renders at its world coordinates,
unscaled by zoom. The reverse (UI on Main) gets culled away when the
camera moves. Authoring Editor-target content in virtual coordinates
renders it at the wrong scale/position (the Editor layer is never
aspect-fit).

## The viewport inset moves compositing and mouse mapping together

`ViewportManager.SetViewportInset(left, top, right, bottom)` reserves chrome
margins (the editor shell) around the game viewport: the aspect-fit
`DestinationRectangle` — and the pixel-perfect rectangle — are computed
inside the remaining centered sub-rectangle, and
`ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates` inverts that **same** rectangle. Because the
`ViewportManager` is the single source of truth, the final-draw compositing
and the cursor's virtual/world mapping can never disagree: a click inside the
inset viewport maps to the correct virtual point with no extra math, and a
click in the margins maps to `null` (`CursorPositionSystem` then flags
`CursorInputComponent.OutsideViewport`; chrome consumes the click in screen
space). An all-zero inset (the default, and `ClearViewportInset`) is
**byte-identical** to the historical full-window letterbox, so every screen
that never sets an inset is untouched. `IntegerScale` and
`PixelPerfectDestinationRectangle` recalculate lazily like
`DestinationRectangle` (a read after a resize/inset change is never stale) —
and `Recalculate` must assign their backing fields directly (reading the lazy
properties inside it recurses). The same single-source-of-truth rule extends
to `DevicePixelRatio` (default 1): when a host renders a device-resolution
backbuffer behind a logically-scaled window (macOS Retina under the editor
run flag — the level-editor module's `EditorHiDpi`), `ScreenWidth/Height`
are DEVICE pixels and `CursorInputSystem` multiplies the raw (logical) mouse
by this ratio, so `ScaleMouseToVirtualCoordinates` keeps inverting the same
space it composites in — at DPR 1 everything is byte-identical.

**Why:** the Wave-7 editor shell renders the game scaled-down in the center
with chrome around it; splitting the inset across two owners (compositor vs
mouse mapping) would desync every world pick by the margin offsets — the
exact class of bug the aspect-fit HUD premise exists for.
**Breaks:** an inset applied to `DestinationRectangle` but not to the mouse
inverse shifts all picking by (left, top); a non-restored inset (screen swap
without cleanup) letterboxes the next screen into a corner; a stale
`PixelPerfectDestinationRectangle` composites the Main layer one
resize/inset behind.
**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/ViewportInsetTests.cs` (zero-inset =
legacy rect + legacy mouse mapping; set+clear restores; inset rect centered
and aspect-correct in the available area; mouse maps inside / nulls in the
margins; resize recomputes; pixel-perfect uses the available area; negative
margins throw; oversized margins clamp).
**Depends on:** "The HUD layer is aspect-fit, not screen-stretched (cursor
depends on it)"; level-editor — "The editor shell insets the game viewport
and renders its chrome at native resolution".

## `MasterRenderSystem` samples per draw type: sprites/meshes PointClamp, text LinearClamp

`MasterRenderSystem` opens a separate `SpriteBatch` for sprites and for text so each gets
its own `SamplerState`. Sprites (and the mesh path) default to `PointClamp` — crisp
nearest-neighbour scaling for pixel art; text defaults to `LinearClamp` — smooth filtering
for bitmap fonts drawn at fractional scale. Both defaults are overridable via the
`spriteSampler` / `textSampler` constructor parameters. Because Sprite and Text are now
distinct batch types, the interleaved renderer flushes + reopens the batch when switching
between them; painter's order is preserved because the draw list is already depth-sorted.

**Why:** a single global `LinearClamp` blurred up-scaled pixel sprites (e.g. a 16×16
indicator drawn at 48×48); a single global `PointClamp` aliases down-scaled bitmap text.
Per-type samplers give each its correct filtering. The mesh path already forced `PointClamp`
(`ResetGraphicsStateForMeshRendering`), so sprites now match it.
**Breaks:** collapsing the Sprite/Text batch split (one sampler for both) forces a single
filter and reintroduces either blurry sprites or aliased text. Passing a non-clamp address
mode would wrap/tile sprites at their edges.
**Tests:** none yet.
**Depends on:** —

## Sprite runs flush below the Reach 16-bit-index budget

`MasterRenderSystem` caps the number of sprite quads submitted between a single
`SpriteBatch.Begin` and its matching `End`. When a contiguous sprite/text run
would push the running quad count past `SpriteBatchFlush.MaxSpritesPerBatch`
(a constant strictly below 5461), the renderer flushes (`End` + `Begin`, with
the same sampler) and resets the count before drawing the next element. Text
elements count one quad per glyph (plus one underline bar per line); a sprite or
pre-expanded nine-patch counts one. The cap is applied on **every** graphics
profile — the renderer contains no `GraphicsProfile` literal or `#if`.

**Why:** MonoGame's / KNI's `SpriteBatch` packs 4 vertices + 6 indices per
sprite; once one batch exceeds 5461 sprites it grows to 32-bit indices, which
the Reach profile (WebGL ES2 / BlazorGL) rejects with `Reach profile does not
support 32 bit indices`. A dense LDtk tile world exceeds 5461 on-screen sprites
even after culling, so without the split it paints on desktop (HiDef) but throws
on web. Splitting unconditionally keeps the engine source platform-agnostic
("the platform is selected by the head") — the head picks Reach vs HiDef; the
renderer never asks.
**Breaks:** removing the cap, raising it to/past 5461, or counting glyph-heavy
text as one quad lets a dense run cross into 32-bit indices and crash a web
build; capping too low pointlessly multiplies draw calls.
**Residual limitation (one draw call cannot be split):** the split happens
*between* draw elements, never *within* one. A single `DrawComponent` whose own
`EstimateSpriteQuads` already exceeds the 5461 hard limit — e.g. a >5461-glyph
text block on one line — is still submitted in one `SpriteBatch.Draw`/`DrawString`,
so it alone crosses into 32-bit indices and throws on Reach. The cap's headroom
(4096→5461) absorbs the conservative text over-estimate of a *normal* element,
not a pathologically huge one. Splitting one `DrawString` is the framework's job,
not the renderer's; if a game legitimately needs a single >5461-glyph run on web,
`TextPrepSystem` (rendering-text) must break it into multiple text entities first.
This residue is out of the splitter's reach by construction.
**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/SpriteBatchFlushTests.cs` — asserts the
cap stays below the 32-bit-index hard limit, that a 20000-sprite run splits into
segments each within the limit with no quads lost, and that text is counted per
glyph. The tests drive the **same** `SpriteBatchFlush.BatchRun` accumulator that
`MasterRenderSystem.RenderInterleaved` uses for its per-element flush decision, so
a regression inside the renderer's loop (dropping the per-`Begin` reset or skipping
the flush check) is reflected in the unit test, not only in an on-device web run.
The desktop demo headless tests
(`MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`) confirm the split is
visually transparent on HiDef.
**Depends on:** foundation — "The platform … is selected by the head project,
never by engine source".

## Mesh indices render through 16-bit indices (Reach-safe)

`MasterRenderSystem.DrawSingleMesh` draws a mesh through the **`short[]`** overload of
`GraphicsDevice.DrawUserIndexedPrimitives`, using the 16-bit index array
`DrawComponent.Get16BitIndices()` returns. Meshes are authored with `int[]` indices
(`MeshData.Indices`, every `IMeshGenerator`), so `Get16BitIndices()` converts once and caches
the result, rebuilding only when `Indices` is reassigned (reference identity changes). It
returns `null` only when the mesh has more vertices than a 16-bit index can address (more than
65536); the renderer then falls back to the 32-bit `int[]` overload, which is valid only on
HiDef. As with the sprite-run flush, the renderer contains no `GraphicsProfile` literal — the
16-bit path is taken on every profile.

**Why:** the overload's index-array type selects the GPU index width (`int[]` ⇒ 32-bit,
`short[]` ⇒ 16-bit), and the Reach profile (WebGL ES2 / BlazorGL) rejects 32-bit indices with
`Reach profile does not support 32 bit indices`. The player's orb is a `CircleMeshGenerator`
mesh; before this, its `int[]` indices took the 32-bit overload and threw on the first web
render tick (it painted on desktop, where HiDef accepts 32-bit). This is the mesh analog of the
sprite-run flush — both keep mesh/sprite submissions inside the 16-bit budget so the engine
source stays platform-agnostic.
**Breaks:** rendering meshes through the `int[]` overload again (e.g. passing `dc.Indices`
directly) reintroduces the Reach crash for every mesh-backed entity — orbs, the demo UI
buttons/checkboxes, physics-demo circles. Converting per frame instead of caching reintroduces
a per-frame allocation that fails the headless heap-flat assertion.
**Caching note:** the cache keys off the `Indices` array reference, not `SetMeshData` — factories
that set `DrawComponent.Indices` directly (e.g. `PlayerEntityFactory`) still get a correct,
rebuilt-on-change conversion.
**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/Rendering/MeshIndexConversionTests.cs` — asserts the short values
match the int indices, that the conversion is cached across calls and rebuilt on reassignment,
that values above 32767 round-trip as unsigned 16-bit bit patterns, and that a mesh past the
16-bit vertex ceiling returns `null` (32-bit fallback). The physics/UI demo headless tests
exercise the mesh path on HiDef; the in-browser physics demo confirms it on Reach.
**Depends on:** foundation — "The platform … is selected by the head project,
never by engine source".

## The draw set is built once per instance, not per frame

A `MasterRenderSystem` instance builds its `EntitySet` (for its `source`)
lazily once and reuses it for the instance's lifetime; it is disposed in
`Dispose`. It must never call `world.GetEntities()...AsSet()` inside the
per-frame `Update`.

**Why:** DefaultEcs's `AsSet()` registers component/entity lifecycle
subscriptions on the `World`, and the World holds those subscription
delegates — which reference the `EntitySet` — alive forever. A set
created per frame is therefore never garbage-collected. An earlier version
built a fresh set every frame, leaking `EntitySet`s every frame, each
retaining its matched-entity array. This is the standing ECS-wide rule
(every other `AsSet()` in the engine is cached in a field) applied to the
renderer. Note that composing N render passes means N cached sets — fine,
because each is built once; two passes with the same `source` (e.g. the
main world pass and a minimap pass) hold two equivalent sets, a negligible
constant cost, not a per-frame leak.
**Breaks:** process memory climbs steadily even on a fully static scene
(no entities or assets added), as observed in the camera and physics
demos. Eventually OOM on a long-running session.
**Tests:** `MonoDreams.Tests/IntegrationTests/HeadlessDemoTests.cs`
asserts a flat live heap across 600 frames of the camera demo (now four
render passes).
**Depends on:** —

## Rendering systems run last in the pipeline

In any screen's pipeline assembly, the prep / cull / sort / render stage
goes at the tail. Logic that mutates renderable state (positions, sprite
source rects, text contents, layer depths) must complete before the prep
module reads it.

**Why:** the prep stage freezes the state of `DrawComponent`s into the
draw queue; mutations after the queue is built are silently lost until
next frame.
**Breaks:** a game system that updates text mid-render-module sees the
old text on screen. A movement system after `CullingSystem` updates
positions without re-culling — entities pop in or out by one frame.
**Tests:** none yet.
